title: New signs of life for NFTs
summary: Data shows new participants minting onchain and new use cases.
body_text: New signs of life for NFTs Data shows new participants minting onchain and new use cases. Variant and Dan Roberts Dec 08, 2023 gm! Don’t call it a comeback: although many have been quick to write off NFTs, the numbers tell a different story. Variant’s resident data scientist Jack Gorman (aka J.Hackworth ) has uncovered data showing NFT interest has actually grown this year, and is primed for broader adoption. The rise of Ethereum layer 2s like Optimism, Base, and Zorachain is a big reason why. Elsewhere, Mason Nystrom explains why humans will soon be using AI bots as an entrypoint into the crypto economy, and Alana Levin makes the case for putting more apps onchain. Enjoy the arrival of the holiday szn, and while you’re thinking about presents, let us suggest you gift this newsletter to your fellow crypto builders and onchain pals. — Dan Roberts , Editor in Chief New Signs of Life for NFTs on Ethereum & L2s Jack Gorman To the outside world, NFTs are dead. When you look at secondary-market sales data—the most commonly cited metric—it's hard to argue. Since the NFT market peak in January 2022, secondary trading volume on Ethereum has fallen by ~90%, and the number of distinct addresses buying an NFT on secondary platforms has fallen by ~82%. September 2023 saw the lowest NFT trading volume and number of buyers on Ethereum since June 2021. But the secondary market (which has been picking up in recent weeks) only paints a partial picture. When you look elsewhere, there are new signs of life for NFTs. One encouraging indicator of NFT adoption is the growth in both creation and collection across Ethereum plus layer-2 solutions such as Base, Zora, and Optimism. For collecting, the number of distinct addresses minting paid NFTs over time has continually grown, suggesting there are new participants minting onchain. The growth in collecting activity has been accompanied by a rise in new NFT contracts on chains like Zora and Base, driven by an array of creator tools that make it easier to create NFTs. While there is certainly some spam and airdrop farming in these numbers, these stats should still be encouraging. One possible explanation for the growth in distinct addresses and new contracts is a simple Occam's Razor view: As more projects, use cases, and art are being created, more cryptonatives are engaging in NFTs. And by lowering the overall financial costs of NFTs, more non-cryptonatives will join in the coming waves. We may also be witnessing a shift in the perception and use cases for NFTs. In the past, rarity, exclusivity, and power-user trading were defining factors of the NFT market, making it harder to onboard more users to crypto. Now, the proliferation of NFTs in various formats and use cases beyond high-end collectibles presents a new opportunity to engage users and promote widespread adoption… Read the rest of the post on our site . title: Historia clínica odontológica: Todo lo que debes saber
summary: Aprende sobre el uso de la historia clínica odontológica, la importancia que tiene en una clínica dental y las ventajas que ofrece su digitalización.
body_text: Tener a la mano la información precisa y completa de tus pacientes es muy importante, sobre todo para el correcto desarrollo de las consultas y el seguimiento de los tratamientos. Para recabar todos los datos de manera estructurada y detallada, cuentas con una gran herramienta: la historia clínica odontológica. ¡Aquí te explicamos qué debes contemplar para evitar omisiones! ¿Qué es una historia clínica odontológica? La historia clínica dental es un registro médico y legal que se usa en odontología para documentar de manera precisa la información sobre la salud bucal del paciente. Este documento incluye los datos personales, el motivo de la consulta, el estado de salud actual, los antecedentes personales, los diagnósticos, las notas de evolución y otros detalles importantes que pueden afectar la atención dental presente y futura. Este expediente clínico es una herramienta esencial en odontología para la atención segura y continua del paciente a lo largo de su vida, definir el mejor diagnóstico teniendo en cuenta la información que está en el documento, establecer el plan de tratamiento más adecuado y poder consultar todos estos datos cuando sea necesario. La historia clínica cumple con un papel legal fundamental al documentar los cuidados prestados. Por ello, es importante que las notas estén con letra legible, sin abreviaturas, tachaduras ni enmendaduras y el documento esté resguardado en buen estado. También tiene una función importante en el área de investigación clínica y epidemiológica . Avanza hacia la odontología digital Transforma tu práctica con tecnología de vanguardia. ¡Empieza ahora y recibe un escáner intraoral gratis! Comenzar ahora ¿Qué datos se recogen en una historia clínica odontológica? Una historia clínica odontológica puede contener diferentes tipos de documentos e informaciones que el dentista considere necesarios: Anamnesis Recoge los datos más importantes del paciente, como el nombre, la edad, fecha de nacimiento, datos de contacto, estado general de salud, hábitos, enfermedades, medicamentos, intervenciones quirúrgicas, entre otros. También incluye el motivo de asistencia a la consulta. Exploración En la historia clínica odontológica se realizan dos tipos de exploraciones físicas: Exploración extraoral: está asociada a la exploración de la estética facial, el análisis de asimetrías o los signos que pongan de manifiesto enfermedades sistémicas. Exploración intraoral: se evalúan los dientes y los tejidos blandos de la cavidad bucal utilizando herramientas especializadas en odontología. En esta revisión, se consideran aspectos como la presencia de caries, enfermedades de las encías, el estado de la higiene bucal, alteración de la estructura dentaria y tratamientos dentales previos. Diagnóstico Con la información de los dos apartados anteriores, el dentista puede emitir un diagnóstico que queda debidamente reflejado en el historial clínico. Pruebas complementarias Las más comunes son la radiografía panorámica, las radiografías parciales (oclusales, periapicales), tomografía, telerradiografía (radiografía lateral del cráneo), análisis cefalométrico. Plan de tratamiento La historia clínica incluye el plan de tratamiento recomendado para alguna patología, la frecuencia de seguimientos que debe tener el paciente o los tratamientos dentales preventivos. Odontograma Es un esquema gráfico de todos los dientes del paciente, identificados cada uno con un número, letra mayúscula o pares numéricos. Esta herramienta presenta tanto la dentición temporal como la dentición definitiva y en el caso de la odontopediatría se usa el esquema de las dos denticiones. En el odontograma se documenta: El estado de la mucosa dental. El estado de cada uno de los dientes: cambio de color, lesiones, si falta el diente. Los tratamientos o restauraciones existentes o por hacer. Evolución de las enfermedades. Si existe dentición temporal o permanente en menores de edad. Periodontograma Es una representación gráfica en la que el periodoncista registra el estado de la encía y lo observado durante la exploración periodontal y en las radiografías: Dientes sanos, prótesis y dientes perdidos. Lesiones. Sangrado o supuración de la encía. Movilidad dental. Placa bacteriana. Margen gingival o profundidad de la bolsa periodontal. De acuerdo con el resultado de la evaluación, el especialista en periodoncia determina la gravedad de la enfermedad periodontal y el tratamiento adecuado. Consentimiento informado Es un documento legal mediante el cual el paciente o su representante legal, una vez que es debidamente informado por el profesional de la salud y son aclaradas sus dudas, de manera voluntaria autoriza la realización de algún procedimiento médico como endodoncia, exodoncia o una fase operatoria. Ventajas de la digitalización en una historia clínica odontológica La digitalización de la historia clínica dental ofrece múltiples beneficios al paciente, la clínica dental y los profesionales de la salud: Simplifica el acceso a la información por parte del médico tratante desde cualquier lugar o dispositivo. Facilita la colaboración interconsulta cuando el médico tratante lo solicite. Asegura la confidencialidad de los datos mediante el cumplimiento de la normativa legal vigente. Permite la personalización de los modelos de historia clínica en función de la especialidad: odontología, periodoncia, endodoncia, ortodoncia, odontopediatría, estomatología, ortopedia maxilar, entre otras. title: Failure Is Expensive
summary: Low prices are tempting, but cheap goods cost far more in the long run
body_text: Home Resources Resources Download Center Guidewire Conversations Podcasts Blog Help and Support Insurance Technology FAQ Blog Blog All Blog Posts Best Practices Careers Customer Viewpoint Developers General Interest Partner Perspective Technology Trends Industry Trends Technology Failure Is Expensive In Terry Pratchett’s 1993 Discworld series novel Men at Arms , a character named Sam Vimes ponders the profound and counterintuitive idea that it is exceedingly expensive to be poor: “The reason that the rich were so rich, Vimes reasoned, was because they managed to spend less money. Take boots, for example. He earned thirty-eight dollars a month plus allowances. A really good pair of leather boots cost fifty dollars. But an affordable pair of boots, which were sort of OK for a season or two and then leaked like hell when the cardboard gave out, cost about ten dollars. Those were the kind of boots Vimes always bought, and wore until the soles were so thin that he could tell where he was in Ankh-Morpork on a foggy night by the feel of the cobbles. But the thing was that good boots lasted for years and years. A man who could afford fifty dollars had a pair of boots that'd still be keeping his feet dry in ten years' time, while a poor man who could only afford cheap boots would have spent a hundred dollars on boots in the same time and would still have wet feet.” This concept has since spawned a broader "boots" theory of socioeconomic unfairness and even a proposal for a basic food price index in the United Kingdom. The basic logic here transcends socioeconomic status. Who among us hasn’t become enamored with a “too good to be true” price tag, only to discover later that we got exactly what we paid for, and then need to make an additional purchase to remedy our prior error in judgment? Pratchett’s insight about boots is also true for kitchen appliances, fishing poles, and construction contractors – pretty much any good or service you can imagine, enterprise software included. And, it’s a natural reaction to have, particularly in an economic environment where inflation (both core and social), scarce reinsurance capital, and increased catastrophe risk are straining insurance carrier budgets. I’ve seen an increasing trend recently of insurance executives who previously chose an overly cost-conscious technology path, only to find themselves unhappy with the outcome. And, the reasons vary. Perhaps it’s a product that does not scale beyond your initial pilot, a lack of functional depth or expertise that causes massive project delays, vendor promises that never materialize, or leadership changes that undercut the prior value case. Having spent hundreds of thousands – or, in some cases, millions – of dollars on solutions that ultimately are not meeting their needs, these leaders are now faced with an even more difficult decision. Do I allow my business to continue struggling with an undeliverable or not-fit-for-purpose solution? Do I prolong the status quo, keeping aligned to our planned technology budget, but with the implicit knowledge that we are leaking significant enterprise value elsewhere? Or, do I bite the bullet, write it all off as a sunk cost, and move ahead on a more reliable and proven path? Am I willing to be wrong and ask for permission to start over? Can I even do that without losing my job? Either way, the ultimate cost is now much higher, both to the executive and to the company, than it would have been to take a longer view at the initial decision point. A more skeptical eye at a made-to-impress price tag, a more thorough interrogation of long-term sustainability, or a heavier weighting on the intangibles of the partnership could have eliminated significant financial and emotional stress over a ten-year planning horizon. So, are really good boots worth five times the cost of cheap boots? That depends on how long you can afford to have wet feet. See More Articles Subscribe to Our Blog

body_text: Cambridge, Mass. – December 21, 2023 – Biobot Analytics, a global leader in wastewater epidemiology, announced that the company has reached full enrollment for a nationwide program sponsored by the National Institute on Drug Abuse (NIDA) to conduct anonymous, population-level wastewater-based monitoring on drugs of use and misuse, and overdose reversal agents. This is the first program of its kind in the United States and follows a design similar to that of successful programs in the European Union and Australia. In less than two months, Biobot recruited 70 wastewater treatment facilities and their associated public health departments into the program, with interest surpassing the program limit. Participants span 43 states, 62 counties representing approximately 35 million Americans, and include a diverse mix of urban and rural communities of varying sizes, ranging from San Diego, CA to Laredo, TX. While few of these communities had previously tested wastewater for high-risk substances, all of them expressed a strong interest in utilizing wastewater data to better understand and prevent substance use disorder and overdose deaths. Throughout this process, Biobot was greeted with high levels of enthusiasm for this program from local officials looking for new and innovative ways to limit the deadly impact of fentanyl and similar substances. In announcing the City of San Francisco’s participation in this initiative , Dr. Hillary Kunins, SFDPH Behavioral Director, explained: “We need all the tools available to identify the presence of substances that may be used to halt and reverse this deadly epidemic. Data from wastewater testing will help provide information about the presence of risky substances in San Francisco and prompt more strategic interventions aimed at saving lives.” “Wastewater surveillance is among public health’s most powerful and sophisticated emerging tools,” said Erie County Commissioner of Health Dr. Gale Burstein, the county representing Buffalo, NY and another participant in the program. “Having access to data and monitoring from Biobot and partners will deepen our understanding of our community’s health trends – particularly around communicable diseases and substance use – while providing actionable data for public health interventions.” Biobot CEO and Cofounder, Mariana Matus, added: “We’re thrilled to see so much momentum and support for wastewater epidemiology not only as a method to track infectious diseases, but also as a valuable tool to combat a range of public health and national security threats, such as the opioid epidemic. Our team will continue to innovate and launch new applications for wastewater in the years to come.” About Biobot Analytics Biobot Analytics is a global leader in wastewater epidemiology, founded with the goal of transforming wastewater infrastructure into real-time public health observatories. Having worked at hundreds of locations across all US states and territories and several countries, Biobot produces actionable information from wastewater to improve the health of communities around the world. Separately from their infectious illnesses work, Biobot also analyzes wastewater for the presence of High Risk Substances , such as opioids, to help communities better respond to substance use and implement harm reduction programming. More information on our mission and technology is available at our website, www.biobot.io .

title: Auditoria de contas a pagar: como preparar corretamente?
summary: Veja como preparar uma auditoria de contas a pagar, quais problemas podem ser revelados e como essa área afeta a gestão de fornecedores da sua empresa
body_text: A auditoria de contas a pagar é uma atividade que verifica minuciosamente todos os pagamentos que a sua empresa fez em um determinado período. Esse processo ajuda a identificar fraudes, desvio de dinheiro, quitações incorretas, ausência de conformidade, entre outros problemas similares. Do ponto de vista de uma gestão de fornecedores eficiente, essa prática contribui para melhorar o relacionamento com esses parceiros comerciais, ao garantir que os valores referentes aos produtos comprados ou serviços contratados estão sendo enviados corretamente e pagos no prazo. Indo mais além, ao analisar de perto as faturas que pagas, é possível identificar se há empresas fornecedoras que não estão devidamente cadastradas na sua base. Quando isso acontece, você abre espaço para riscos como os financeiros e até mesmo jurídicos. Aliás, a garantia de compliance é um dos benefícios de auditorias de contas a pagar. Porém, para usufruir dessa vantagem e de outras, é fundamental preparar adequadamente esse tipo de auditoria. Não sabe como fazer isso? Siga a leitura deste artigo e descubra agora mesmo! O que é auditoria de contas a pagar? **A auditoria de contas a pagar é um processo realizado para revisar e avaliar todas as faturas, contas, boletos e demais documentos que foram pagos por uma empresa durante um determinado período. Os principais objetivos dessa prática é identificar inconformidades e garantir que os pagamentos sejam feitos corretamente. ** Apesar de essa prática estar diretamente relacionada à gestão financeira, ela também tem importante peso na área de compras e procurement. Aqui, podemos partir do princípio de que os fornecedores são participantes importantes nas estratégias de crescimento de qualquer companhia. Sem eles, não há a base necessária para a produção e comercialização dos itens que geram renda para o negócio. Uma boa política de pagamento de fornecedores garante que esses parceiros sejam pagos em dia. Esse cuidado é fundamental para estreitar e melhorar o relacionamento entre eles e sua empresa. Por outro lado, quando esse fluxo não funciona corretamente, a tendência é haver problemas contratuais, desentendimentos, perda de um importante apoio estratégico e, por fim, danos reputacionais e financeiros para o seu negócio. Uma das maneiras de evitar transtornos como esses é realizando uma auditoria eficiente na área de contas a pagar. Dica de leitura: “ Auditoria de campo: entenda o que é, qual sua importância e como implementá-la na sua empresa ” Quais os principais problemas revelados por auditorias de contas a pagar? E já que estamos falando sobre evitar problemas, os principais que podem ser identificadas em um processo de verificação como esse são: documentos perdidos : como boletos e faturas que não foram arquivados corretamente, seja em arquivos físicos ou em digitais (na nuvem); pagamentos incorretos : especialmente os feitos a mais que não foram apontados pelos credores; fornecedores não registrados : a exemplo daqueles que foram contratados para atender uma emergência e que, por esse motivo, não foram criteriosamente qualificados; gargalos no fluxo de pagamento : tais como excesso de burocracia, envio das faturas para diversos responsáveis a fim de obter aprovação, entre outros relacionados; falhas nos registros financeiros : especialmente quando essa atividade é realizada manualmente; inconformidade : como o pagamento incorreto de impostos, tanto para mais quanto para menos, que pode gerar diversos transtornos com os órgãos fiscalizadores. Ao descobrir problemas como esses você tem a chance de solucioná-los. Com isso, melhora a produtividade dos times e eleva a eficiência da área financeira. Quais os benefícios de auditorias de contas a pagar na gestão de fornecedores? Além desses dois pontos positivos que acabamos de citar, ao auditar a área de conta a pagar existem diversos outros benefícios que podem ser percebidos no seu negócio. Inclusive, eles refletem bastante na gestão de fornecedores . Os principais são: cumprimento do SLA (Acordo de Nível de Serviço) firmado com as empresas fornecedoras; aprimoramento do relacionamento com os fornecedores , contribuindo para a formação de parcerias estratégias; melhor aproveitamento do orçamento destinado para compras e procurement; fortalecimento da imagem da marca perante os stakeholders, ao honrar os compromissos financeiros assumidos; garantia de conformidade regulatória , evitando problemas e gastos com os órgãos reguladores. Como preparar uma auditoria de contas a pagar? Para preparar corretamente a auditoria de contas a pagar, e usufruir de todos os benefícios que essa prática gera, o passo a passo mais indicado a ser seguido é: defina quando a auditoria será realizada; levante todos os documentos, dados e registros que serão apurados; faça uma reunião pré-auditoria 1. Defina quando a auditoria será realizada Ao definir que as contas a pagar da sua empresa precisam ser auditadas, os funcionários não precisam ser “pegos de surpresa”. Na verdade, é importante informá-los sobre a data que essa verificação acontecerá, para que tenham tempo de se preparar adequadamente. Esse prazo varia de acordo com o tipo de auditoria, que pode ser interna ou externa. O primeiro formato é executado por profissionais da sua empresa que não têm ligação com essa atividade, a fim de garantir a imparcialidade. Na segunda opção é preciso contratar auditores terceirizados e alinhar a agenda do seu negócio com a deles. Não deixe de ler este artigo: “ Comitê de auditoria: o que é, como funciona e como implantar ” 2. Levante todos os documentos, dados e registros que serão apurados Tudo o que se relaciona a contas a pagar precisa ser acessado facilmente para ser apresentado aos auditores tão logo eles solicitarem. Por isso, antes da data da auditoria, levante todos os boletos, faturas, comprovantes de pagamento, entre outros documentos referentes ao período que será analisado. Relatórios com os registros do que foi pago também ajudam bastante nesse momento. Assim, o ideal é gerá-los antes do início da verificação. 3. Faça uma reunião pré-auditoria É comum os funcionários, e até mesmo os gestores, ficarem nervosos durante as auditorias. Uma forma de amenizar esse sentimento é realizando uma reunião pré-auditoria. Aproveite o momento para explicar como será o processo, os objetivos dessa verificação mais precisa e quais podem ser os benefícios para a rotina de todos e para a empresa em uma visão geral. Sugestão de artigo para você: “ Como fazer checklist de auditoria de fornecedores? Para que serve? ” Como fazer a otimização da auditoria de contas a pagar? É quase impossível otimizar algum processo sem contar com ajuda da tecnologia. title: Willis Carrier & 5 Others You Can Thank For Air Conditioning | Chart Industries
body_text: Back to Articles Willis Carrier & 5 Others You Can Thank For Air Conditioning Chart Industries | December 12, 2023 The sun is beating in through the window, a bead of sweat appears on your forehead. You have so much to do today you need to remain focused. But the heat? It’s too much. Solution? Blast the air con. You can thank Willis Carrier for that, well not just him, him and 5 other individuals that between themselves discovered and developed air conditioning which now benefits so many people and industries across the world. Most commonly used to keep an interior environment, like an office or store, at an optimal and comfortable temperature. But can be used across a range of industries and sectors like hospital operating theatres, nuclear power facilities, or underground in mines , even museums of fine art to IT data centres. But how did we get here? This blog is going to talk to you about the ‘Father of Air Conditioning’ Willis Carrier, and 5 other key figures that you can thank for air conditioning. Let's start at the beginning... 1. (&2.) Benjamin Franklin and John Hadley In 1758, Benjamin Franklin, yes the founding father of the United States of America, along with John Hadley, a chemistry professor at Cambridge University, conducted the first documented test for the theory of air conditioning - to test the principle of evaporation as a means to rapidly cool an object. By placing various liquids on the bulb end of a mercury thermometer they discovered that the temperature would drop as the liquid evaporated - therefore the evaporation of liquids causes heat loss. They were able to lower the temperature of a mercury thermometer from 64 degrees Fahrenheit down to 7 degrees Fahrenheit, and noted that blowing on the liquid would make it evaporate quicker. Another thing that they noted was that more volatile liquids such as alcohol and ether had a greater cooling effect, with the capabilities to drive down the temperature of an object past the freezing point of water. Franklin concluded: "From this experiment one may see the possibility of freezing a man to death on a warm summer's day." - Sounds like a more extreme version of modern air conditioning to us! 3. Michael Faraday Next up in 1820, the English scientist and inventor Michael Faraday discovered that if you compressed ammonia, turning it to liquid, that when that liquid later evaporates it would chill the air inside the room. Faraday continued on to become one of the most influential scientists in history, discovering the chemical benzene and inventing an early form of the Bunsen burner to name but a few of his successes. Even Albert Einstein kept a picture of Faraday on his study wall. 4. John Gorrie In 1842, the Florida physician John Gorrie built his ice-making machine - a machine that used compressor technology to compress air and water to make ice. It then had air blown over the ice which in turn cooled the air in the room, keeping his patients nice and cool. In 1851 he gets his ice-making machine patented and envisions a world full of his machines keeping everyone cool all over the world. Sadly, Gorrie lacked the financial backing and died in 1855 - along with his dream of commonplace air conditioning. Until, “The father of air conditioning” came along. Willis Carrier “The Father of Air Conditioning” Willis H Carrier, who from 1902 to 1915 was Chief Engineer of the Buffalo Forge Company, subsequently acquired by Howden in 1993, invented the first electrical air conditioning unit in 1902. Carrier was left with the task to improve the manufacturing process in a printing plant that suffered from excessive humidity, which wreaked havoc on the inks used to print. To remedy this Carrier submitted drawings of a system that would control temperature, control humidity, control the air circulation and ventilation, and cleanse the air - not bad for a 25 year old fresh out of college. Using his knowledge of heating objects with steam, he simply reversed the process. Instead of sending air through hot coils, he sent it through coils filled with cold water instead. As the air cooled, moisture in the air increased, therefore the humidity, along with the temperature could be controlled. And thus, the modern air conditioner was born. Using aeration here means that grit is more efficiently removed, reducing any problems that grit can cause in the processes further downstream. Selected blowers will deliver maximum efficiency - check out our selection of blowers here. 5. Stuart W Cramer Deserving an honorary mention. Stuart Cramer. In 1906 while exploring ways to add moisture to the air in his textile mill, Stuart Cramer invented a ventilating device that combined moisture with ventilation that “conditioned” the air in his factories. By adding water vapour to the air he was able to control the humidity making the textiles easier to work with. He coined this process “air conditioning” and Wills Carrier liked it so much he adopted the term and even incorporated it into the name of his company. So there we have it, the discovery and development of the modern air conditioner and who you have to thank for it.

body_text: Home / About AE / News & Events / Blog / Dynamic Reverse Pulsing – What About the Anode? Dynamic Reverse Pulsing – What About the Anode? Posted December 04, 2023 by Gayatri Rane A previous AE blog, Dynamic Reverse Pulsing – What About Duty Cycle? , discussed reactive sputter deposition of insulating thin films in large-area coaters, describing the benefits of using the Dynamic Reverse Pulse (DRP) power-delivery mode over the bipolar (BP) mode of dual magnetron sputtering. In DRP mode , dual targets are bipolar pulsed against an explicit anode and the duty cycle can be varied so that the polarity is positive on the target for a shorter time during pulsing. This allows clearing of charge build-up on the targets. In our studies, DRP mode showed increased deposition rate and reduced substrate temperature when compared to similar depositions with the BP mode. Understanding the Effect of the Anode The main difference between DRP mode and BP mode is the presence of an explicit anode in the former. To understand the effect of the anode further, we designed new tests to study the effect of increased anode area and their placement on the deposition process and film properties. Figure 1 shows 2 anode configurations that were compared in an industrial drum coater. In the first case, the two targets were pulsed against the single anode bar present between the two targets (1-anode configuration). In the second case, the two targets were pulsed against three anode bars — one present between the two targets and the other two on either side of the targets (3-anode configuration). Figure 1: Placement of anodes and target for DRP testing. In 1-anode configuration, only anode number 1 was used. In 3-anode configuration, anodes number 1, 2 and 3 were connected together. The equivalent circuits are shown on the right. Tw Ascent AP DMS power supplies were used for these tests, each powered to 6 kW. The Si targets were sputtered at a total power of 12 kW in an Ar/N2 gas mixture to deposit silicon nitride thin films on glass. The Ar flow was fixed to 100 sccm. Table 1 provides the tested DRP settings (duty cycles and pulsing frequencies). The discharge voltage variation as a function of N2 gas flow is shown in Figure 2 for the 1-anode and 3-anode configurations. For each DRP setting, the discharge voltage was slightly higher for the 3-anode configuration compared to the 1-anode configuration. Optimization tests revealed that 130 sccm of N2 gas flow was required to deposit stoichiometric and transparent silicon nitride films with refractive index of 2.05 at 550 nm (measured with ellipsometer). 500 nm thick films were deposited with Ar:N2 flow of 100:130 sccm for the above DRP settings to compare their properties. Figure 3 shows the results for the power-normalized dynamic deposition rate (ellipsometer measurement), thermal load at the substrate (thermocouples attached on glass substrate) and residual stress in the films (substrate curvature method). Comparing the 1-anode and 3-anode configurations, we observed a10% increased deposition rate,10% decreased thermal load at the substrate and lowered residual stress with the 3-anode configurations. Figure 3. Deposition rate, temperature rise at the substrate and residual stress in silicon nitride films deposited with DRP mode in 1-anode and 3-anode configurations. Representative error bars are indicated. Optical emission spectroscopy (OES) was also employed in these studies for process monitoring. For this, two OES collimator heads were placed in with one head facing the plasma in front of one target and the other head facing the plasma in front of anode-1 between the two targets. The placements of the heads are as shown in Figure 4, looking at the plasma from the top down. The intensities of the Ar (825 nm) line and the N (337 nm) line are shown. In the 3-anode configuration, the intensities of all the lines are, in general, reduced. Besides this, the intensity of the N line in the plasma in front of the target decreased while that of Ar remained unchanged. These results indicate a more diffuse spread of the plasma in the 3-anode configuration. Thus, answering one aspect of our question about the anode, we observed appreciable improvements in thin-film properties upon increasing the anode surface area in DRP mode and observed a difference in the plasma spread. These results also indicate the importance of anode placement. We are continuing to delve deeper into DRP mode, including researching anode placement, and will keep you updated as we learn more. title: The Role of Customer Feedback in Subscription Billing Improvement
summary: This blog explores the significance of customer feedback in the realm of subscription billing, delving into how businesses can harness this valuable resource to enhance their billing systems.
body_text: In the dynamic landscape of subscription billing, customer feedback stands as a pivotal compass, guiding businesses towards continuous improvement and customer-centric practices. This blog explores the significance of customer feedback in the realm of subscription billing, delving into how businesses can harness this valuable resource to enhance their billing systems and foster long-term customer satisfaction. Understanding the Customer Perspective To improve subscription billing, businesses must first comprehend the customer experience. Customer feedback provides invaluable insights into how users interact with billing processes, pinpointing pain points, and revealing areas for enhancement. This understanding forms the foundation for strategic improvements that align with customer expectations. Identifying Billing Pain Points Customer feedback acts as a diagnostic tool, helping businesses identify and address billing pain points. Whether it's unclear pricing structures, inconvenient payment methods, or complicated invoicing, feedback offers a direct line to the challenges customers face. This information is crucial for refining billing systems to be more user-friendly and efficient. Enhancing Transparency and Communication Transparent communication is key to customer trust. Feedback highlights instances where communication fell short or was unclear. By addressing these concerns, businesses can improve transparency in billing, ensuring customers are well-informed about charges, billing cycles, and any changes to their subscription plans. Streamlining the Billing Process Efficiency is paramount in subscription billing. Customer feedback sheds light on bottlenecks and complexities within the billing process. Armed with this information, businesses can streamline their billing procedures, making it easier for customers to manage their subscriptions, update payment details, and navigate billing-related tasks. Iterative Improvements Based on Feedback Customer feedback should be viewed as a continuous feedback loop rather than a one-off exercise. Businesses can implement iterative improvements based on ongoing feedback, ensuring that the billing system evolves alongside customer needs and technological advancements. This iterative approach creates a dynamic and responsive billing environment. Cultivating Customer Loyalty Through Responsive Action When customers see that their feedback leads to tangible improvements, it fosters a sense of loyalty. Acknowledging and acting upon customer suggestions or concerns demonstrates a commitment to providing an excellent subscription experience. Loyal customers are not only more likely to continue their subscriptions but may also become advocates for the business. The Power of Positive Feedback Positive feedback is as valuable as constructive criticism. Customers who have positive experiences with the billing process can provide insights into what is working well. Understanding these strengths allows businesses to reinforce successful practices, creating a positive feedback loop that enhances the overall customer experience. Case Studies in Customer Feedback-Driven Improvements Case Study 1: Netflix Netflix, a pioneer in streaming services, continually refines its subscription billing based on customer feedback. The introduction of personalised subscription plans, clear billing communication, and user-friendly account management features are outcomes of Netflix's responsiveness to customer input. Case Study 2: Amazon Prime Amazon Prime, a subscription service offering a range of benefits, actively seeks customer feedback to enhance its billing processes. Amazon's responsive approach has led to improvements in billing transparency, options for subscription customization, and proactive communication about upcoming charges. In the subscription billing landscape, customer feedback isn't just a resource; it's a strategic imperative. By actively seeking, analysing, and acting upon customer feedback, businesses can create billing systems that align seamlessly with customer expectations. This commitment to continuous improvement not only ensures a smooth billing experience but also positions the business as customer-centric and responsive in an ever-evolving subscription economy.

title: What is Review Management? The Complete Guide to Manage Reviews Effectively
summary: Review management is how brands monitor, respond to, and act on customer reviews at scale. Get the 2026 framework, AI workflows, benchmarks, and templates.
body_text: Key Takeaways: Review management is the ongoing system of monitoring, responding to, and acting on customer reviews, and it now directly shapes revenue, search visibility and brand trust. A single unanswered review costs more than it looks, because consumers read your responses, reward brands that reply and quietly walk away from those that stay silent. Reviews are scattered across Google, Trustpilot, G2, app stores and social channels, so consolidating them into one view is the difference between control and chaos. AI now reads sentiment, spots emerging issues early and drafts responses at a scale no manual team can match, freeing people for the judgment calls that matter. Fast, personalized responses backed by clear time benchmarks protect reputation far better than a flawless-looking profile ever could. Review management is how brands monitor, respond to, and act on customer reviews across every platform where people talk about them. It sounds simple until you're the one staring at a one-star review that landed an hour ago, a dozen more scattered across Google, Trustpilot, and the app stores, and a customer base that has already read them. 97% of consumers read online reviews before buying from a local business, so those few paragraphs strangers wrote about you now shape revenue more directly than most of your marketing. The problem isn't a lack of feedback; it's the volume and the speed. Reviews arrive around the clock, on channels your team may not even monitor, and the cost of silence is real: failing to respond can raise customer churn by 15% . This guide breaks down what review management actually is, why it now sits at the center of brand and revenue strategy, where reviews live, a step-by-step framework, how AI has changed the game, and the benchmarks and templates you can use today. Table of Contents What is review management? Importance of review management Key platforms where customer leave reviews How to manage online reviews? A step-by-step framework How is AI enhancing review management? Best practices to manage online reviews Final Thoughts What is review management? Review management is the ongoing practice of monitoring, responding to, analyzing, and acting on customer reviews across every channel where they appear, from Google and Trustpilot to G2, app stores, and social platforms. Done well, it is not a reactive support task but a coordinated system that protects online reputation management , improves the product, and turns customer feedback into measurable business value. In practice, it covers four connected jobs: Listening for new reviews in real time Replying quickly in a consistent brand voice Resolving the underlying issue Feeding recurring themes back to the teams who can fix them The shift in 2026 is that these jobs no longer sit in one inbox; they span marketing, customer service, and product, which is exactly why brands need a single view of it all. Is review management the same as reputation management? No, though they overlap. Review management is a focused discipline: monitoring and responding to customer reviews on sites like Google, Trustpilot, and G2. Reputation management is broader, covering everything that shapes public perception, including news, social sentiment, search results, and executive visibility. Think of review management as one core pillar of a wider reputation strategy, and usually the highest-frequency one. Importance of review management Reviews are no longer just social proof , they are a financial signal. A one-star improvement in a business's average rating can lift revenue by 5-9% , and 95% of consumers say positive reviews make them willing to pay more. On the flip side, 94% of customers say a negative review has convinced them to avoid a business altogether. What tips the balance is not perfection; it is responsiveness. 89% of consumers read a business's responses to reviews before deciding and 45% pay close attention to which companies bother to reply. Yet only about 5% of businesses actually respond to their reviews — making a disciplined response habit one of the cheapest competitive advantages available. It now reaches the boardroom too: in PwC's 2025 CEO survey, 84% of executives ranked brand and reputation risk as their top external concern, ahead of cyber and regulatory risk. Do fake reviews really affect a business? Yes, and increasingly so. Roughly 30% of online reviews are now estimated to be fake, and 62% of consumers are concerned about AI-generated reviews. That skepticism cuts both ways: shoppers now distrust a flawless five-star profile, and only about 20% fully trust a brand that shows nothing but praise . Actively managing reviews, reporting fakes, and responding transparently to genuine criticism is what keeps a profile credible. Key platforms where customer leave reviews Reviews are fragmented across dozens of destinations, and Google alone hosts roughly 57 to 58% of all online reviews, with 81% of consumers checking it first. But your buyers rarely stop there. The platforms that matter most fall into a few groups: General and local discovery: Google Business Profile, Facebook, Yelp, and Apple Maps, where local intent and star ratings drive foot traffic and clicks. Consumer trust marketplaces: Trustpilot, Sitejabber, and the Better Business Bureau, which carry weight for e-commerce and service brands. B2B software review sites: G2, Capterra, TrustRadius, and Gartner Peer Insights, where enterprise buyers vet vendors before shortlisting. Commerce and app ecosystems: Amazon, the Apple App Store, and Google Play, where product ratings directly gate conversion. Industry-specific hubs: TripAdvisor and Booking.com for travel, Healthgrades and Zocdoc for healthcare, Glassdoor for employer reputation, and Zomato or DoorDash for food. The takeaway isn't to be everywhere manually; it's to consolidate them. Bringing every source into one view through social listening is what makes review management possible at scale. How to manage online reviews? A step-by-step framework Managing reviews well is not about reacting faster to whatever shakes loudest. It is about running the same disciplined loop every time, so nothing slips; and every review feeds the next decision. Here are the six steps that turn scattered feedback into a system. Step 1: Centralize monitoring across every platform You cannot manage what you cannot see, and the average brand reviews are spread across Google, Trustpilot, G2, Yelp, app stores, and half a dozen social channels. The first move is to pull all of them into a single dashboard with real-time alerts, so a new review triggers action within minutes instead of surfacing days later when the damage is done. This matters because recency is now a trust signal in itself: 73% of consumers only trust reviews written in the last 30 days, so a review that sits undetected is not just a missed reply; it is aging into irrelevance while shaping opinions you never got to influence. Step 2: Prioritize and route by sentiment and urgency Not every review deserves the same response speed and treating them equally is how the important ones get buried. Use sentiment analysis to triage automatically: a furious one-star review from a high-follower account, a safety or compliance complaint, and a mild three-star note about slow shipping all need different owners and different clocks. Route service issues to support, product bugs to engineering, and legally sensitive cases to the right escalation path, so each review lands with the person who can actually resolve it rather than sitting in a shared inbox no one owns. Step 3: Respond quickly, personally, and in a consistent brand voice Once a review is in the right hands, the response itself is where trust is won or lost. Acknowledge the reviewer by name, reference the specific thing they raised, and reply in a voice that sounds like a person, not a policy. The trap at scale is consistency curdling into copy-paste: a wall of identical replies signals a brand going through the motions, and readers notice. The goal is responses that are uniform in tone and standards but visibly specific to each customer, which is exactly the balance AI-assisted drafting now makes achievable across hundreds of reviews a week. Related Read: How to Respond to Customers on Social Media (+ Examples) Step 4: Resolve the issue and close the loop A reply is a promise; a resolution is what keeps it. For anything beyond a simple “thank you”, move the conversation to a private channel, fix the underlying problem, and follow up to confirm the customer is satisfied. This step is the one most programs skip, and it is the most valuable: prompt, genuine resolution is repeatedly rated the single most effective way to rebuild trust after a bad experience, and a meaningful share of customers will edit or upgrade a negative review once they feel genuinely heard. Publicly noting that an issue was resolved also reassures every future reader who finds that review later. Step 5: Analyze patterns and feed them back to the business One review is an anecdote; fifty reviews saying the same thing are a roadmap. The highest-value output of review management is not the individual response; it is the pattern, the recurring complaint about a checkout step, a shipping partner, or a specific store that is quietly costing you customers. Cluster themes across platforms, quantify them, and route those customer feedback insights to the teams who can act, whether that is product, operations, or a regional manager. This is the moment review management stops being reputation defense and starts driving real improvement. Step 6: Generate more authentic reviews, deliberately The most durable defense against a handful of loud critics is a steady stream of genuine positive reviews that reflects your actual customer base. Ask at the moments of peak satisfaction, after a smooth delivery, a resolved ticket, or a renewal, and remove every ounce of friction with direct links and simple prompts. Volume and freshness compound: products with five or more reviews convert far better than those with none, and a regular flow of recent reviews keeps your overall rating representative rather than skewed by whoever happened to be angriest that month. Should you respond to positive reviews too, or only negative ones? Respond to both. Negative reviews are urgent, but positive reviews are an easy win most brands ignore: a quick, specific thank-you reinforces loyalty and signals to future readers that the brand is present. A good rule is to respond to 100% of negative reviews and a healthy share of positive ones, prioritizing detailed or influential praise. How is AI enhancing review management? Manual review management breaks the moment volume scales. A single enterprise brand can field thousands of reviews a week across dozens of platforms and languages, far more than any team can read in time, let alone answer. AI closes that gap not by replacing judgment, but by doing the mechanical work underneath it. Four capabilities matter most in 2026: Sentiment and intent detection, in context. Modern natural language models read beyond keywords, catching sarcasm, slang, mixed emotion, and emojis across 100-plus languages, and scoring each review as positive, negative, or neutral the moment it lands. That is what makes real-time triage possible instead of manual reading. Anomaly and crisis detection. Rather than waiting for a manager to notice, AI watches the baseline and flags an unusual spike in negative sentiment, often the earliest warning of a product fault or PR issue, while there is still time to get ahead of it. Theme clustering at scale. Instead of ten thousand separate opinions, AI groups reviews into the handful of themes actually driving your rating, turning an unreadable firehose into a short, prioritized list any team can act on. Agentic, on-brand response drafting. The newest shift is generative AI drafting context-aware, brand-voice replies for agents to approve in seconds, and increasingly handling routine responses autonomously within set guardrails, so humans focus on the sensitive, high-stakes cases. Pro tip: Sprinklr Insights is built for exactly this. Its AI-native social listening pulls reviews and mentions from 1B+ websites and review sites alongside 30+ social channels, applies 40+ industry-trained AI models to score sentiment and surface emerging themes, and routes each review to the right team automatically, so your people act on the patterns that move brand health instead of reading every line. The payoff shows up in real operations. Deutsche Bahn , Europe's largest rail operator, handles up to one million inbound messages a year across social and review channels. By unifying monitoring and response on Sprinklr, it cut case processing time by 17% and case handling time by 49% , proof that AI-assisted management scales responsiveness without scaling headcount. Best practices to manage online reviews Knowing the framework is one thing; running it to a standard is another. Reference the exact issue and use the reviewer's name. Templated-sounding responses do more harm than no reply at all, because they tell every future reader that no one actually read the complaint. Handle sensitive details privately by phone or email, then post a short public note confirming it was sorted. Future customers judge you less on the complaint and more on how you handled it. Managed well, that feedback becomes the most honest research your brand has: a live map of what to fix, what to double down on, and where trust is being won or lost in real time. Managed poorly, or ignored, it becomes a slow leak in reputation and revenue that no marketing budget can fully patch. The brands that will pull ahead are not the ones with flawless ratings; they are the ones that respond the fastest, sound the most human, and actually change based on what they hear. That is only sustainable when a disciplined human touch is paired with AI that can watch, interpret, and route at a scale people cannot. title: Data exfiltration from Writer.com with indirect prompt injection
body_text: Data exfiltration from Writer.com with indirect prompt injection Authors: PromptArmor and Kai Greshake PromptArmor Dec 15, 2023 This vulnerability can allow attackers to steal a user’s private documents by manipulating the language model used for content generation. As of now, it has not been fixed as it was not triaged as a security vulnerability by Writer.com after disclosure (more details in Responsible Disclosure section at the end). Edit 12/19/2023: It is no longer possible to render markdown images or clickable links in Writer.com . (the attack, disguised in white text on an attacker controlled website) Writer.com is an application that can be used by enterprises and consumers alike. Users can upload data files, share links, and ask questions in order to generate tailored content for their business needs. It has access to your brand and knowledge base and as such can maintain consistency when writing articles for you. They emphasize its data security given the sensitivity of information its clients upload throughout its website: https://writer.com/product/data-security-privacy/ (screenshot from writer.com/security on Dec 13) (screenshot from writer.com on Dec 5) 1. The vulnerability: In Writer, users can enter a ChatGPT-like session to edit or create their documents. In this chat session, the LLM can retrieve information from sources on the web to assist users in creation of their documents. We show that attackers can prepare websites that, when a user adds them as a source, manipulate the LLM into sending private information to the attacker or perform other malicious activities. The data theft can include documents the user has uploaded, their chat history or potentially specific private information the chat model can convince the user to divulge at the attacker's behest. This type of attack is called indirect prompt injection , initially coined by Kai Greshake. To prove the feasibility of such an attack, we uploaded a file that contains mocked sensitive information (SSN numbers, revenue figures, salary information), and were able to exfiltrate all of it: (screenshot from our pentesting exfiltration server) The website that hosts the payload looks like any other website, and the payload is hidden from any user visiting it. In the following screenshot, the hidden text of the payload is highlighted (it has white font, but there are other methods to hide it or embed payloads on other websites such as social media platforms).: (screenshot from the website with the injection) Note that *.cloudfront.net is one of the locations allowed by the CSP. 2. A Complete Attack Chain A typical user use case would be the following: However, here’s what actually happens in the background with the injection A) They ask Writer to write a report for them based on some sources and some data they upload. (screenshot from our chat session at writer.com) B) They find a nice source on the web which has the information they need C) They upload some sensitive data D) They get Writer to write the report (screenshot from our chat window at writer.com) E) Writer reads the webpage, but it contains a hidden injection in small white text: F) Writer follows the instructions, and overrides the initial instructions of the user and any security filters Writer.com has enforced. The user never asked for this image and it was not on the webpage that they initially asked for. Nevertheless, Writer.com has automatically rendered the attacker-controlled image in markdown and you can see in the network activity that it has appended the contents of the uploaded client data file to the HTTP parameters, just as instructed: (screenshot of our chat session at writer.com with network activity expanded) Here’s a side by side comparison between the uploaded client data file, and a zoomed in image of the HTTP parameters from the above screenshot: G) Without their knowledge, their data has now been exfiltrated to the attacker’s server. Rendering the image in markdown automatically created a GET request with the HTTP parameters including the content of the file. The attacker can read their logs to extract the sensitive client data from the file. (screenshot from pentesting exfiltration server logs) Rendering an image to exfiltrate data is only one method of exfiltrating data. Note that while, to our knowledge, Writer does not use OpenAI for text generation, OpenAI has said the same issue in their system is a “won’t fix.” Please see below for other example attacks which use other mediums (like links) to exfiltrate data. Additional Examples: Example 1: Exfiltration of uploaded files In this example, an attacker is able to exfiltrate a confidential file that the user uploads via a link, using this injection: Video explanation (sent with disclosure) Example 2: Exfiltration of chat history In this example, an attacker is able to exfiltrate the chat history from a user via a link, using this injection: Video explanation (sent with disclosure) Putting this in context: These type of attacks have been done in other LLM surfaces, such as the Bard attack by Thacker, Rehberger and Greshake , which was resolved promptly by the Google Security and Bard team. For more information on these attacks and relevant information here are some great sources: https://kai-greshake.de/ (twitter: @KGreshake) https://embracethered.com/blog/index.html (twitter: @wunderwuzzi23) https://josephthacker.com/ (twitter: @rez0_) https://promptarmor.com/ (twitter: @promptarmor) And to learn more about LLM security risks feel free to check out: https://owasp.org/www-project-top-10-for-large-language-model-applications/ https://atlas.mitre.org/ Responsible Disclosure Timeline Nov 29: We disclose issue to CTO & Security team with video examples Nov 29: Writer responds, asking for more details Nov 29: We respond describing the exploit in more detail with screenshots Dec 1: We follow up Dec 4: We follow up with re-recorded video with voiceover asking about their responsible disclosure policy Dec 5: Writer responds “We do not consider this to be a security issue since the real customer accounts do not have access to any website.” Dec 5: We explain that paid customer accounts have the same vulnerability, and inform them that we are writing a post about the vulnerability so consumers are aware. No response from the Writer team after this point in time. Dec 15: This post is published on Hacker News Dec 19: We are informed that this particular data exfiltration method (markdown image rendering and clickable links) is no longer viable. See more research from PromptArmor’s threat intelligence team at promptarmor.com/#threatintel, and from Kai Greshake at kai-greshake.de/about Disclaimer: The content of this blog is intended solely for research and educational use, aimed at enhancing knowledge, understanding, and awareness regarding attacks and their countermeasures to bolster the security of Large Language Models (LLMs)
